Meccan, and it has forty-five verses [it was revealed after al-Furqan]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Fatir al-samawat (Originator of the heavens): its originator and innovator. From Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "I did not know what Fatir al-samawati wal-ard (Originator of the heavens and the earth) meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: 'I originated it' [[mentioned earlier at the beginning of al-An'am]], i.e., I began it."

It was also read: ﴿Alladhi fatara al-samawati wal-ard wa ja'ala al-mala'ikah﴾ (He who originated the heavens and the earth and made the angels). And it was read: jai'il al-mala'ikah (Maker of the angels), in the nominative, as a form of praise.

Rusulan (messengers), with the sin pronounced with a damma or with a sukun (both readings are possible), uli ajnihah (possessors of wings): possessors of wings. Ulu is a plural noun of dhu (possessor), just as ula'ika is a plural noun of dha (this). Their parallels in the declinable category are al-makhad (the pregnant she-camels) and al-khilfah (the she-camels in their ninth month).

Mathna wa thula wa ruba' (two, three, and four) are descriptive modifiers of ajnihah (wings). They are not declined (do not take tanwin) only because the principle of 'adl (deviation from the regular form) is repeated in them. That is, they have deviated from the forms of the cardinal numbers into other forms, just as ʿUmar deviated from ʿĀmir, and Hadhdham from Hadhimah, and from repetition to non-repetition. As for the descriptive quality, the situation does not differ between the deviated form and the form from which it deviated. Do you not see that you say: "I passed by four women" (niswatin arba') and "by three men" (rijalin thalathah), and no attention is paid to it?

The meaning is: the angels are of various kinds [[his statement "that the angels, of kinds" is probably "varied in creation, etc." (Editor)]]: some of them have wings two by two, that is, each one of them has two wings; some have wings three by three; and some have wings four by four. Yazidu fi al-khalqi ma yasha' (He adds to creation whatever He wills): that is, He increases in the creation of wings and in other things whatever His will and wisdom require. The original is two wings, since they stand in the place of hands; then the third and fourth are an addition to the original, and that is stronger for flight and more helpful for it. If you say: the pattern of pairs of wings is that each side should have half of them, so what is the form of three? I say: perhaps the third is in the middle of the back between the two wings, supporting them with strength; or perhaps it is for something other than flight. It has been related to me in some books that a kind of angel has six wings: two with which they wrap their bodies, two with which they fly on Allah's errands, and two hanging over their faces out of shyness before Allah.

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) on the night of the Mi'raj, and he had six hundred wings [[agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his form, which had six hundred wings; and the wording of Ibn Hibban is: "I saw Jibril near Sidrat al-Muntaha, and he had six hundred wings spreading pearls and rubies from his feathers"]]. It is also related that he asked Jibril (peace be upon him) to appear to him in his form, and he said: "You will not be able to bear that." He said: "I love that you do it." [[Ibn al-Mubarak related it in al-Zuhd, and al-Tha'labi from his route: al-Layth related to us from ʿAqil from al-Zuhri with this. He added: "And al-Wass is a small sparrow, so that it cannot carry his throne except as its bulk."]] Al-Wasʿ, with a fatha on the ṣād, followed by an unmarked (ḥamlah) letter, also unmarked. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out on a moonlit night, and Jibril came to him in his form, and the Prophet ﷺ fainted. Then he recovered, and Jibril (peace be upon him) was supporting him, with one of his hands on his chest and the other between his shoulders. He said: "Glory be to Allah! I did not think that any of creation was like this." Jibril said: "Then how would it be if you saw Israfil? He has twelve wings: one wing in the east and one in the west. The Throne is on his shoulder, and he shrinks at times out of the greatness of Allah until he becomes like the wasʿ, which is the small sparrow." [[his statement "like the wasʿ, which is the sparrow": in al-Sihah, "al-wasʿ" is a bird smaller than the sparrow (Editor)]]

It is related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿Yazidu fi al-khalqi ma yasha'﴾: "It is a beautiful face, a beautiful voice, and beautiful hair." It was also said: "beautiful handwriting." From Qatadah: beauty in the eyes. The verse is unrestricted and encompasses every increase in creation: height of stature, balance of form, completeness of the limbs, strength in grasping, soundness of intellect, [[his statement "soundness" means firmness (ihkam), as stated in al-Sihah (Editor)]] nobility of opinion, boldness of heart, generosity of soul, fluency of tongue, and eloquence in speech [[his statement "eloquence in speech" means skill, as stated in al-Sihah (Editor)]], good deliberation in handling affairs, and what is similar to that, which description cannot encompass.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verse 2:

The word "fath" (opening) is borrowed for "release" and "sending forth." Do you not see His saying ﴿so none can release it after Him﴾ in place of "none can open it for Him"? Meaning: whatever mercy Allah releases, that is, any blessing of provision, rain, health, security, or other kinds of His favours, which cannot be counted. The indefiniteness of "mercy" (raḥma) is for generality and vagueness, as if He said: "from whatever mercy there is, heavenly or earthly; no one can hold it back or restrain it, and whatever Allah withholds, no one can release." If you ask: why is the pronoun first made feminine, then mentioned as masculine at the end, when it refers in both cases to the noun that implies the meaning of a condition? I say: these are two usages, treating the word according to its meaning and according to its wording, and the speaker has the choice between them. So he made it feminine according to the meaning of "mercy," and made it masculine because the word referred back to has no feminine marking. Also, since the first was explained as "mercy," it was good to make the pronoun follow the explanation, while the second was not explained, so it was left in its original masculine form. It has also been read as ﴿fa-la mursila lahā﴾ (feminine).

If you ask: the second must have an explanation, so what is its explanation? I say: it may be that its explanation is like the explanation of the first, but it is omitted because it is indicated by it; or it may be general, covering whatever He withholds of His wrath and His mercy. The first was explained and not the second only to show that His mercy precedes His wrath. If you ask: what do you say about the one who explained "mercy" as "repentance" and attributed this to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father? I say: if he means by repentance guidance to it and enabling in it, which is what Ibn 'Abbas intended if he said it, then it is acceptable; but if he means that if the sinner wills to repent he repents, and if He does not will it he does not repent, then it is rejected, because Allah the Exalted always wills repentance [[His saying "He always wills repentance": this and what follows is according to the Mu'tazila view, that it is obligatory upon Him, exalted is He, to do what is best for the servant.

According to the Ahl al-Sunna, nothing is obligatory upon Him, so the statement is on its apparent meaning, and that interpretation is rejected. (ʿA)]]. And it is not permissible for Him not to will it ﴿after Him﴾, that is, after His withholding, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Who then can guide him after Allah?﴾ ﴿In what discourse after Allah, then, will they believe?﴾ That is, after His guidance and after His signs. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, the Overpowering, the One able to send and withhold, ﴿the Wise﴾, who sends and withholds what wisdom requires He send and withhold.

The purpose of mentioning the blessing is not merely to mention it verbally, but to do so with the tongue and the heart together, to guard it against ingratitude and contempt [[The phrase "guarding it against ingratitude and contempt": i.e., belittling it. Al-Sihah (by al-Jawhari) provides this definition. (ع)]], and to thank for it by knowing its due, acknowledging it, and obeying its Giver. From this is the saying of a man to one he has favoured: "Remember my favours to you." He means: guard them, thank for them, and act upon what they require. The address is general to all people, because all of them are immersed in Allah's blessing. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: he means, "O people of Makkah, remember Allah's blessing upon you, in that He settled you in His sanctuary and protected you from the whole world, while people are being snatched away from around you" ﴿and people are being snatched away from around you﴾ [Qur'an 29:67]. And he also said: "Allah's blessing is well-being."

It is recited as "ghayru Allah" with all three vowels: the genitive and the nominative as a qualifier, both in wording and in grammatical position, and the accusative as an exception. If you ask: what is the grammatical position of "yarzuqukum" (who provides for you)? I answer: it may have a grammatical position when you make it a qualifier of "Khaliq" (Creator), and it may have no grammatical position when you make it an explanation (tafsir) and take "min khaliq" (a creator) as nominative in position by a verb implied by this, as if it were said: "Does a creator other than Allah provide for you?", or when you make "yarzuqukum" an independent sentence.

[Mahmud said: "If you say, 'What is the grammatical position of yarzuqukum?' I answer: it may have a position if you make it a qualifier of Khaliq, and it may not have a position if you make it an explanation and take min khaliq as nominative in position by a verb implied by this, as if it were said: 'Does a creator other than Allah provide for you?' or you make yarzuqukum an independent sentence." Ahmad said: the last of these is the most likely.]

And it may have no grammatical position if you put "min khaliq" in the nominative, with "yarzuqukum" implied, and make "yarzuqukum" an explanation of it, or make it an independent sentence after the words ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah?﴾ [Qur'an 35:3].

If you ask: does this contain evidence that the term "Creator" is not applied to anyone other than Allah, Exalted is He?

[His words continue: "If you ask: does this contain evidence that the term 'Creator' is not applied to anyone other than Allah? I answer: yes, if you make yarzuqukum an independent sentence, which is the third of the three possibilities. As for the other two, namely the qualifier and the explanation, the term is restricted in them by provision from heaven and earth, and it has left the unrestricted sense. So how can it be cited as proof of its negation absolutely?"

Ahmad said: when this verse strikes the ears of the Qadariyya (the school that holds human beings create their own acts), they say, with boldness against Allah, Exalted is He: "Yes, there is a creator other than Allah, because everyone in their view creates the act of himself." For this reason you see al-Zamakhshari widen the circle, bring forward the scattered and repelling readings, and make both readings agree with his belief in the existence of a creator other than Allah. Their reading is the true and apparent one, and he placed it last in mention to show his bias. What confirms the third reading, and that it is what is meant, is this: the verse was addressed to a people who were polytheists, and when they were asked about their provider from heaven and earth, they said, "Allah." So they were made to affirm this and were rebuked by it, as a establishing of proof against them through their own confession. If it were in any other form, restricted, its implied meaning would be the affirmation of a creator other than Allah who does not provide, but these disbelievers have already disavowed that, so there is no point in rebuking them with something that fits their own statement. The third reading is preferred from the standpoint of the purpose of the context of the verse. As for the verbal structure, the two clauses, "yarzuqukum" and "la ilaha illa Hu" (there is no god but Him), are joined in one flow, and the second is separated by agreement from what precedes it, and so is "wa-zinatuha" (and its adornment).]

If you make "yarzuqukum" an independent sentence, yes. This is the third of the three possibilities. As for the other two, the qualifier and the explanation, the term may be restricted in them by provision from heaven and earth, and it has left the unrestricted sense. So how can it be cited as evidence for its exclusiveness to Allah, in its unrestricted sense? The provision from heaven is rain, and the provision from earth is plants. ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a separated sentence with no grammatical position, like "yarzuqukum" in the third reading. If you joined it as you joined "yarzuqukum," the meaning would not support it, because your saying, "Is there any other creator besides Allah, there is no god but that creator," is not correct, for your saying, "Is there any creator besides Allah?" is an affirmation of Allah, so if you went on to say that, you would be contradicting an affirmation with a negation. ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ [Qur'an 35:3], that is, from what direction are you being diverted from monotheism to polytheism?

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verse 4:

He thereby censures the Quraysh for their poor reception of the signs of God and for their denial of them, and he consoles His Messenger (ﷺ) that he has, in the prophets before him, a good example (uswah hasanah). Then He brings what contains both promise and threat: the return of all affairs to His judgment, and the recompense of the one who denies and of the one who is denied, each according to what they deserve. It is also recited as "turja'" (tarja'), with the "ta'" vowelled with a damma and with a fatha. If you ask: what is the correct sense of the conditional's answer (jaza' al-shart)? Its requirement is that the answer follow the condition, whereas this (clause) precedes it. I say: its meaning is: "And if they deny you, then take consolation (fa-ta's) in the denial of the messengers before you," so that "fa-qad kudhdhibat rusulun min qablika" is placed in the position of "fa-ta'assa," dispensing with the consequence by means of the cause, namely, denial in place of consolation. If you ask: what is the meaning of the indefiniteness in "rusul"? I say: its meaning is "messengers have indeed been denied," namely, messengers of great number and multitude. And (there were) possessors of signs and warnings, people of long lives, and companions of patience and resolve, and what is similar to that. This is more consoling to him and more urging toward perseverance.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verses 5–7:

Allah promised those who obey Him reward, and threatened those who disobey Him with punishment. ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾, that is, let it not deceive you, and let not the enjoyment of it and the pleasure of its benefits distract you from working for the Hereafter and seeking what is with Allah. ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you about Allah﴾, that is, let him not say to you: "Do whatever you wish, for Allah is Forgiving, who forgives every grave sin and pardons every wrongdoing." [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: let not Satan say to you: 'Do whatever you wish, for Allah is Forgiving, who forgives every grave sin and pardons every wrongdoing.'" Ahmad said: He is alluding to the Ahl al-Sunnah (the adherents of the Sunnah, the Sunni community) in their belief that Allah may forgive grave sins for the one who professes God's oneness (al-muwahhid), even without repentance.

This does not contradict the truthfulness of Allah's promise, because when Allah threatened [punishment] for grave sins, He attached the promise to His will, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. So they, when they affirm the promise of Allah, are certain of it according to what has been reported.]]. Al-Gharur is Satan, because deception is his constant practice. It has been read with a damma, al-Ghurūr, which is a verbal noun of gharra, like al-luzum and al-nahuk, or the plural of gharr, like qā'id and qu'ūd.

Allah informed us that Satan is a clear enemy to us, and He related to us his story and what he did to our father Adam, peace be upon him, and how he took it upon himself to be an enemy to our kind from before its existence and after it. We, despite this, take him as a guardian and obey him in what he wants from us, which is our destruction. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, admonished us: since you know your enemy, than whom there is no enemy more deeply rooted in enmity, yet you treat him as one who has no knowledge of his condition, then ﴿take him as an enemy﴾ in your beliefs and your actions, and let there come from you nothing but what shows opposition to him and hostility toward him, in your secret and in your open conduct. Then He summarized the essence of his affair and the error of those who follow him: his aim, which he intends in calling his partisans and those who follow his footsteps, is to bring them to the place of wretchedness and destruction, and that they become among the companions of the blaze. Then He removed the veil and stripped away the bark [[His saying "and stripped away the bark": in al-Sihah (the dictionary of al-Jawhari), al-lihā' (with a long vowel) means the bark of a tree. (ʿ)]], to cut off vain hopes and false wishes, and so He built the whole matter upon faith and deeds, and their abandonment.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verse 8:

When he mentioned the two groups, those who disbelieved and those who believed, He said to His Prophet: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good...?﴾ Meaning: is one of these two groups whose evil deed has been made attractive to him the same as one for whom it has not been made attractive? It is as if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said "No." Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, so do not let yourself go to waste in regret over them.﴾

The meaning of making deeds attractive and of misguidance is one and the same: that the disobedient person is in a state in which beneficial considerations are of no use to him, so that he deserves thereby the abandonment of Allah the Exalted, His leaving him to himself. At that point he wanders in misguidance, lets loose the command and prohibition, embraces obedience to desire, until he sees the ugly as beautiful and the beautiful as ugly, as if his mind has been overpowered and his discernment stripped away. He takes his stand under the words of Abu Nuwas:

"Give me to drink until you see me
finding the ugly beautiful to me.
We hide it, so it comes
with a fine scent that spreads."

"Give me to drink until you see me..." by Abu Nuwas. "We hide it" means the wine, "so it comes" means its scent, "spreads" means its fragrance. Then he says to the wine-server: "Give me to drink until I become intoxicated, so that the ugly seems beautiful to me." "Beautiful" is the second object, and "the ugly" is its subject; finding it beautiful is a metaphor for the intensity of intoxication.

When Allah abandons those who are resolved upon disbelief and leaves them to themselves, the Messenger must not be concerned about their affair, nor pay heed to mentioning them, nor grieve or be consumed with sorrow over them, following the Sunnah of Allah the Exalted in abandoning and leaving them. Al-Zajjaj mentioned that the meaning is: "Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him [like one guided]? Your soul would have gone out in regret over them," so the answer is omitted, being indicated by "so do not let your soul go to waste over them." Or: "Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him like one whom Allah has guided?" so the answer is omitted, being indicated by "Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills." ﴿Hasarat﴾ is an object of purpose: meaning, "do not destroy yourself for the sake of regrets."

﴿Alayhim﴾ is a complement of "tadhhab" (go to waste), as you say: "he perished over him in love," and "he died over him in grief." Or it is an explanation of what is regretted.

It is not permissible for it to be linked to ﴿hasarat﴾, because a verbal noun cannot precede its complement. It is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal), as if all of them had become regrets because of the intensity of grief, as Jarir said:

"The noontide heat and the night journey wasted their flesh,
until they went, mere breastbones and chests."

Jarir describes she-camels as emaciated. It is said: a horse is "mamshuq," meaning tall and lean; a girl is "mamshuqa," meaning slender of frame. "Al-Hajira" is the intensity of heat. "Al-Sura," with a dammah, is travel by night. "Al-kulkul" and "al-kulkal" mean the chest, and the conjunction of "al-suduur" with "al-kulkul" is explanatory: that is, from the intensity of heat and travel they became as mere bones with no flesh on them.

He means: they returned as mere breastbones and chests, that is, nothing remained but their breastbones and chests. From the same usage is his saying:

"Following them, my soul falls away
in regrets, and remembering them is a sickness for me."

When grief befell him after the departure of the beloved and took firm hold of his soul, he imagined that his soul was scattering and falling from his body in successive regrets, and he made the soul into regrets because it was mingled with them, so that it was them. Or: "it falls away after them because of regrets and sorrows," and this is more apt. "Dhikruhum" means their remembrance is a sickness for me; it is with a fatha, a verbal noun like "suqm" (sickness).

It is also read: ﴿Do not let your soul go to waste.﴾ ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾: a warning to them of punishment for the evil of their conduct.

Also read: "arsala al-riyah" (He sends the winds). If you ask: why does "fa-tuthiru" come in the present tense, unlike what precedes and follows it? I say:

So as to depict the state in which the winds stir up the clouds, and to bring before the mind those marvellous images that point to the divine power. They do this with an act that carries some distinction and particularity, in a situation that is strange or that concerns the listener, or otherwise, as Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said:

"Indeed I met the ghoul, as she was descending
into a level plain, like a page, a flat expanse,
So I struck her without fear, and she fell
prostrate, on her hands and on her neck."

Here the verse is a poem by Ta'abbaṭa Sharran:

"Indeed I met the ghoul, as she was descending
into a level plain, like a page, a flat expanse,
So I struck her without fear, and she fell
prostrate, on her hands and on her neck."

Ta'abbaṭa Sharran's poem. Al-ghawl: the female of the devils. Al-ʿiyān: seeing with the eye. Al-hawā: descending. The meaning is: speed of running.

Al-sahb (with fatḥa): the wide, level open ground with distant edges. Al-ṣaḥīfa: the book. Al-ṣaḥṣaḥān and al-ṣaʿṣaʿān (with fatḥa): the level ground. Al-jarān (like kitāb): the front of the neck bone from the throat to the chest hollow; its plural is jirna (like kutba) and ajrina (like afʾida). He says: whoever denies the existence of the ghoul has lied, for I report with certainty. It is also permitted that the meaning is: "O you who deny the existence of the ghoul, I report with a report arising from certainty, which is what is established by conclusive proof, indeed by direct sight and observation with the eye, that I met her running in a wide, level place." He repeated the description for emphasis, and placed the explicit noun where a pronoun would be expected, to firmly fix the ghoul in the listener's mind and to inspire awe. The expected phrasing would be "fa-darabtuhā," but he shifted to the present tense to depict a past state as though it were present and visible now, so that it is marvelled at and his bravery is known; that is: "so I began striking her without fear, and she fell cast down upon her hands and neck." The form faʿīl is applied to both masculine and feminine, as here.

Because he intended to portray for his people the state in which he, in his own claim, was emboldened to strike the ghoul, as if showing it to them and informing them of its reality, so that they might marvel at his courage in the face of every terror and his steadfastness in every hardship. Likewise the driving of the clouds to a dead land, and the reviving of the earth with rain after its death: since these are among the signs of overwhelming power, it says "fa-sachnā" and "aḥyaynā" (We drive, We revive), turning them away from the third-person form to what is more closely tied to exclusivity and more indicative of it. The kāf in kadhālika is in the nominative position, meaning: like the reviving of dead land is the resurrection of the dead.

It is related that it was said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "How does God revive the dead, and what is the sign of that in His creation?" He said: "Did you pass by the valley of your people when it was barren, and then pass by it again when it was stirring with green?" He said: "Yes." He said: "So God revives the dead, and that is His sign in creation." (Al-Khāzin has "yahtazz" in place of "yahuzz" here. — Ṭībī's note.) Some say: God revives the creation with water that He sends from beneath the Throne, like the seed of men, from which the bodies of creation grow.

Those who disbelieved used to seek strength through idols, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [19:81]. As for those who believed with their tongues without their hearts being in agreement: they used to seek strength through the polytheists, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honor with them? Indeed, honor belongs wholly to Allah﴾ [4:139]. So He made clear that there is no honor except with Allah and His allies. He also said: ﴿But honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [63:8]. The meaning is: let him seek it from Allah. The words ﴿honor belongs wholly to Allah﴾ were put in place of that phrase, dispensing with it because they indicate it, since a thing is sought only from its owner and possessor. A parallel to this is your saying: "Whoever wants counsel, it is with the righteous," meaning: let him seek it from them, but you have placed what indicates it in its position. The meaning of ﴿honor belongs wholly to Allah﴾ is that all honor is exclusive to Allah: the honor of this world and the honor of the Hereafter. Then He made known that what honor is sought through is faith and righteous deed, by His saying: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [35:10]. The "good word" is: there is no god but Allah. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: this means that these words are not accepted, and they do not ascend to heaven to be written where accepted deeds are written, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyun﴾ [83:18], unless they are accompanied by a righteous deed that realizes them and confirms them, and then it raises them and makes them ascend. It has also been said: the one who raises is the word, and what is raised is the deed, because no deed is accepted except from one who professes the oneness of Allah. It has been said: the one who raises is Allah, exalted is He, and what is raised is the deed. It has also been said: the good word is every remembrance: glorifying takbir (Allahu akbar), tasbih (subhan Allah), tahlil (la ilaha illa Allah), recitation of the Qur'an, supplication, seeking forgiveness, and other things. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is the saying of a man: Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar. When the servant says it, an angel carries it up to heaven and it gives life to the face of the Most Merciful. But if there is no righteous deed, it is not accepted from him,"[[Recorded by al-Tha'labi and Ibn Marduwayh through the narration of 'Ali ibn 'Asim, from Suhayl, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet. Al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma', and al-Tabari also narrated it, traced to Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]] And in a hadith: "Allah does not accept a saying except with a deed, and He does not accept a saying or a deed except with intention, and He does not accept a saying, a deed, and an intention except in conformity with the Sunnah."[[Recorded by al-Khatib in al-Jami', through the narration of Baqiyyah ibn Isma'il ibn 'Abd Allah, from Aban, from Anas, in this form, traced to the Prophet. Aban is abandoned (matruk). It has another chain from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet, recorded by Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Hibban, both in al-Du'afa', through Khalid ibn 'Abd al-Da'im, from Nafi' ibn Yazid, from Zuhrah ibn Ma'bad, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from him, with the wording: "A Qur'an recitation in prayer is better than a Qur'an recitation outside prayer," to the end of the hadith, in which is: "and no saying except with a deed," etc. Ibn Hibban also narrated it through al-Zuhri, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Ibn Mas'ud, and in its chain is Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Misri, who is a liar.]] " And it is related from Ibn al-Muqaffa': "A saying without a deed is like broth without fat, a cloud without rain, and a bow without a string."

It has been read: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ in the passive form, and ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ in the active form, from "aṣʿada" (to cause to ascend). The one who causes it to ascend is the person, meaning: the good word ascends to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the good speech ascends to Him. It has been read: ﴿and the righteous deed raises it﴾, with the deed in the accusative, and the one who raises is the word, or Allah, Mighty and Majestic. If you say: makr (plotting) is an intransitive verb; one does not say "makara fulan 'amalahu" (so-and-so plotted his deed), so with what is ﴿evil﴾ (al-sayyi'at) in the accusative?

I say: this is an adjective of the verbal noun, or of what is in its position, as in His saying: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾ [35:43]. The original is: "those who plotted the evil plottings." Or: "kinds of evil plotting." By these He meant the plottings of Quraysh when they gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (Assembly House) and deliberated about one of three plots they would plot against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): either to confine him, or to kill him, or to expel him, as Allah, glorified is He, related of them: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you﴾ [8:30]. ﴿And the plotting of those, it will perish﴾ [35:10]: meaning, the plotting of those who plotted those three plots is exclusively what perishes, that is, it is wasted and corrupted, unlike the plotting of Allah against them, when He expelled them from Makkah, killed them, and fixed them in the well of Badr. So He gathered all their plottings upon them and fulfilled in them His saying: ﴿And they plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters﴾ [8:30], and His saying: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people.﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verse 11:

"Azwājan" (kinds, categories), or males and females, like His saying ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾ [42:50]. And on the authority of Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with him: "He paired some of them with others." "Bi-ʿilmihi" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: except that it is known to Him.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿and none is granted a long life, nor is anything taken off his life﴾? I answer: its meaning is "and none of anyone is granted a long life." He called him "one granted a long life" on account of what he is coming to. If you ask: a human being is either one granted a long life, i.e. long-lived, or one whose life is shortened, i.e. short-lived. As for one being subject to both granting of length and its opposite in succession, that is impossible, so how is His saying ﴿and none is granted a long life, nor is anything taken off his life﴾ valid? I answer: this is from the kind of speech that is lenient in its usage, relying on the hearers' understanding of its interpretation, and depending on their correct grasp of its meaning by their intellects, and that it will not be confused for them that lengthening and shortening in one life are contradictory. And upon this is the widespread speech of people: they say, "Allah does not reward a servant or punish him except with right."

[[Quoted verse of poetry]] "And I have never found favour in a land nor found it disagreeable without my sojourn there being brief." [[Note: his saying "and I found it disagreeable (ijtawaytuhu) without my sojourn being brief" means: I disliked staying in it, as in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]

There is another interpretation: that a person's life is neither lengthened nor shortened except in a Book. Its form is that it is written on the Preserved Tablet: "If so-and-so performs Hajj or fights in jihad, his life is forty years; and if he performs Hajj and fights, his life is sixty years." When he combines them and reaches sixty, he has been granted a long life. And if he does one of them alone and does not exceed forty, then his life, which is the limit of sixty, has been shortened. To this the Messenger of Allah ﷺ alluded in his saying: "Indeed, charity and maintaining ties of kinship build up dwellings and increase lifespans." [Narrated by Ahmad through al-Qasim from ʿAʾishah, but he said "good character" instead of "charity," and al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Shuʿab by this route likewise, adding "and good neighbourliness." It has another route in al-Asbahani from Abu Saʿid with the wording "maintaining ties of kinship, good character, and kindness to parents," and added "even if the people are wicked."]

And on the authority of Kaʿb, when ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, was stabbed, he said: "If ʿUmar had asked Allah, He would have deferred his term." [Narrated by Ishaq at the end of the Musnad of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, Mamar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from Said.]

It was said to Kaʿb: "Has not Allah said ﴿when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor advance it﴾ [7:34]?" He said: "Allah has said ﴿and none is granted a long life﴾."

It has spread on people's tongues: "May Allah prolong your survival," and "May your lifespan be extended," and the like.

On the authority of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is written in the record, his lifespan is so-and-so years, and then written beneath it: a day has passed, two days have passed, until it reaches its end."

On the authority of Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with him: "The one granted a long life is one who reaches sixty years, and the one whose life is shortened is one who dies before sixty years." "Al-kitab" means the tablet. On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is also permissible that "the Book of Allah" is meant as the knowledge of Allah, or the record of the person.

It is read "wa-la yunqaṣu" (with the verb active), with the subject being "min ʿumrihi," with the lightened form.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verse 12:

He struck the two seas, the sweet and the salty, as examples of the believer and the disbeliever. Then he said, by way of digression (*istitrad*), in describing the two seas and what is attached to them of His blessing and bounty: ﴿And from each of them you eat fresh flesh﴾, meaning, from each one of the two, you eat fresh flesh, which is fish, ﴿and extract ornaments﴾, which are pearls and coral, ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it﴾, meaning, in every ship cleaving the water with its movement. It is said: *makhrat al-safinah al-ma'*, "the ship cut through the water." And the clouds are called *banat makhr*, "daughters of cleaving," because they cleave the air. The *sufun* (ships), from which the word *safinah* (ship) is derived, is close to *makhr*, because they skim (*tasfunu*) the water as if peeling it, just as they cleave it. ﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾, meaning, of the bounty of God. No mention of it has occurred in the verse itself, but it has occurred in what precedes it, and had it not occurred, it would not be problematic, since the meaning points to it. The particle of hope (*harf al-raja'*) is used figuratively for the meaning of intention (*al-iradah*). Do you not see how it takes the path of the lam of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), as if it were said: "so that you may seek," and "so that you may give thanks."

*Al-Furat* is that which quenches thirst. *Al-sa'igh* is that which is pleasant and easy to swallow because of its sweetness. It was read as *sayigh* on the pattern of *sayyid*, and as *sayigh* with lightening (*takhfif*). *Milh* is on the pattern of *fa'l*.

*Al-ajaj* is that which burns with its saltiness. It is also possible, apart from the path of digression, that the two kinds (the believer and the disbeliever) are compared to the two seas, and then the salty sea is preferred over the disbeliever, in that it shares with the sweet sea in benefits, such as fish and pearls, and the ships move through it, while the disbeliever is devoid of benefit. This is in the manner of His saying, ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones, or even harder in hardness﴾ (2:74), and then He said, ﴿And indeed among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed among them are those that split and water issues from them, and indeed among them are those that fall down from fear of God﴾ (2:74).

Dhalikum (ذلكم) is the subject (mubtada'). "Allahu rabbukum" and "lahu al-mulk" are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifah). Alternatively, "Allahu rabbukum" consists of two predicates (khabarān). The clause "lahu al-mulk" is a new nominal sentence (jumlah mubtada'ah) occurring in the context of the words ﴿And those you invoke besides Him possess not even a qitmir﴾.

In terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), it is also permissible for the name Allah to be a qualifier (sifah) of the demonstrative (ism al-isharah), or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), with rabbukum as the predicate (khabar).

But the meaning rejects this. Al-qitmir is the membrane wrapped around the date pit, the thin skin that clings to it.

If you call upon the idols, they will not hear your call, because they are inanimate objects. And even if they did hear, by way of supposition and illustration, they would not respond to you, because they do not accept the divinity you ascribe to them, and they disown it.

It is also said that the meaning of "they will not respond" is that they will not benefit you. "They will disown your associating them with God" [[The phrase "they will disown your associating them with God" seems to have lost its explanation. In al-Nasafi: "They will disown your associating them with God: your making them partners and your worshipping them, and they will say: 'You did not worship us'; and none will inform you like one who is well-acquainted (with the matter)." (Ed.)]] and "none will inform you like the One who is All-Aware." That is, the All-Aware alone is the one who informs you of the truth, to the exclusion of all other informants. The meaning is: what I have told you about the state of the idols is the truth, because I am All-Aware of what I have told you.

It is also read: "yad'ūn" (they call upon), with the letter ya' and with the letter ta'.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verses 15–17:

If you ask: why were "the poor" (al-fuqara') defined with the article? I answer: by this he intends to show them that, because of their intense need for Him, they are the very genus of the poor, even though all creatures, among humankind and others, are in need of Him, because poverty follows from weakness, and the weaker the needy one is, the poorer he is. Allah, glory be to Him, has testified to man's weakness in His saying: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [4:28], and He, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿It is Allah who created you from weakness﴾ [30:54]. Had it been indefinite, the meaning would be "you are some of the poor."

If you ask: the poor have been set against the self-sufficient (al-ghani), so what is the benefit of ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ (al-Hamid)? I answer: when He established their need for Him and His self-sufficiency from them, and not every self-sufficiency is beneficial unless the self-sufficient one is generous and bestowing, then when He is generous and bestows, the one He bestows upon praises Him and He becomes deserving of praise from them, He mentioned "the Praiseworthy" to indicate that He is the self-sufficiency whose self-sufficiency benefits His creatures, the Generous who bestows upon them, and who, by His bestowing upon them, deserves that they praise Him, the Praiseworthy on the tongues of their believers.

﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ [14:20 / 35:17 context]: that is, not impossible for Him (bi-'aziz: bi-mumtani', "not unattainable" or "not beyond reach"). This is a threat against them for their taking rivals (andad) to Him, their disbelief in His signs, and their disobedience, as He said: ﴿And if you turn away, He will substitute a people other than you﴾ [47:38].

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that He will create after you those who worship Him and do not associate anything with Him.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verse 18:**

*al-wizr* and *al-wiqr* are two related words, and *wazara al-shay'* means he carried the thing. *Wazira* is a descriptive attribute of the soul (*nafs*). The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection every soul bears only its own burden, the sin it has committed. No soul is seized for the sin of another soul, unlike the tyrants of this world who seize the close kinsman for the kinsman and the neighbour for the neighbour. If you ask: why was it not said, "no soul bears the burden of another"?

Why was *wazira* said? I answer: because the meaning is that the bearing souls (*al-nufus al-wazirat*) are not seen, none of them, except bearing its own burden and not the burden of another. If you ask: how do you reconcile this with His saying ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ (29:13)? I answer: that verse concerns the misguided who misguide others. They bear the burdens of misleading people along with the burdens of their own misguidance, and all of that is their own burden; there is nothing in it of the burden of anyone else. Do you not see how God refuted their saying ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ (29:12), by His saying ﴿but they will not bear anything of their sins﴾ (29:12)?

If you ask: what is the difference between the meaning of His saying ﴿No bearer bears the burden of another﴾ (6:164; 35:18) and the meaning of ﴿If a burdened one calls to its load, nothing of it will be carried﴾ (35:18)? I answer: the first indicates the justice of God in His judgment, and that He does not hold a soul accountable for the sin of another. The second indicates that on that day there is no one to give aid to one who seeks aid, to the extent that a soul weighed down by sins and crushed by them, if it called for some of its weight to be lightened, would not be answered and would not be relieved, even if the one called upon were one of its close relatives, a father, a son, or a brother.

If you ask: to what does *kāna* in ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾ (35:18) refer? I answer: to the one called upon, understood from His saying ﴿If a burdened one calls﴾. If you ask: why was mention of the one called upon omitted? I answer: so that it generalizes and includes every one who is called upon. If you ask: how is it correct to leave the general term implicit, when the general term cannot be the near relative of the burdened one? I answer: it is of the generality that occurs by way of substitution (*al-badal*). If you ask: what do you say about the one who recited ﴿وَلَوْ كانَ ذا قُرْبى﴾ with *kāna* as a complete verb (*kāna al-tāmma*, "kāna" meaning "to exist"), as in His saying ﴿and if one is in hardship﴾ (2:280)? I answer: the arrangement of the speech is better suited to the incomplete *kāna* (*kāna al-nāqisa*, the copula), because the meaning is that if the burdened one calls someone to carry her load, nothing of it will be carried, even if the one called is a near relative. This is a sound meaning and coherent. If you said, "even if a near relative were found," it would fall apart and depart from its consistency and coherence. [[His saying "and it departed from its consistency and coherence," meaning: its organization. (ʿ)]] Moreover, here there is something that permits a pronoun to be hidden in the verb, unlike what you have cited.

*bil-ghayb* is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) either from the subject or from the object. That is, they fear their Lord while absent from His punishment, or they fear His punishment while it is absent from them. It has also been said: *bil-ghayb* means in secret. This is the attribute of those who were with the Messenger of God ﷺ among his companions, whose constant habit was to fear God. They are the ones who established the prayer and treated it as a raised beacon and an elevated sign. The meaning is: you can only warn these people and caution them from your people, and you can only obtain the benefit of the warning among them, not among their rebellious ones and their obstinate people.

﴿And whoever purifies himself﴾, meaning whoever purifies himself by performing acts of obedience and abandoning acts of disobedience. It is also read *wa-man azkā fa-innamā yuzkā*, and this is an interjected clause that emphasizes their fear and their establishing of the prayer, since these are part of purification. ﴿And to God is the final return﴾ is a promise of reward to those who purify themselves.

If you ask: how is ﴿You only warn﴾ connected to what precedes it? I answer: when He showed His anger against them in His saying ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾ (35:16), He followed it with a warning about the Day of Resurrection and mention of its terrors. Then He said ﴿You only warn﴾, as if the Messenger of God ﷺ had made them hear that, but it did not benefit them. So ﴿You only warn﴾ was revealed, or God informed him of His knowledge concerning them.

The blind man and the seeing man are a parable for the disbeliever and the believer, just as the two seas were given as a parable for them, or for the idol and Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The darkness and the light, the shade and the scorching heat, are two parables for truth and falsehood, and for what each of them leads to in reward and punishment. The living and the dead are a parable for those who entered Islam and those who did not enter it and persisted in disbelief. Al-harur is al-samum (the scorching wind), except that al-samum occurs by day, whereas al-harur occurs both by night and by day. It is also said that it occurs by night specifically.

If you say: what is the lā that is followed by the conjunction wāw? I say: when the wāw falls within a negation, it is joined to it to emphasize the meaning of negation. If you say: is there any difference between these wāws? I say: some of them join an even pair to an even pair, and some join an odd one to an odd one.

Inna Allaha yusmi'u man yasha' means: He knows who will enter Islam among those who will not enter it, so He guides the one whom He knows that guidance will benefit, and forsakes the one whom He knows that guidance will not benefit. As for you, their affair is hidden from you, and therefore you are eager and keen for the Islam of a people among the forsaken. Your case in this is like that of one who wants to make the deaf hear and warn them, and that is not something that can be done. Then He said: in anta illa nadhir, meaning: your only duty is to convey and warn. If the one warned is among those who hear the warning, it benefits him; and if he is among the persistent, then you bear no blame.

Bil-ḥaqq (بِالْحَقِّ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from one of the two pronouns, meaning: "truly" or "as two truthful ones" (muḥaqqan aw muḥaqqīn). Alternatively, it is an attribute of the verbal noun (ṣifah lil-maṣdar), meaning: a sending accompanied by the truth. Or it is a complement (ṣilah) of bashīr and nadhīr, so that the sense is: a bringer of good news of the true promise, and a warner of the true threat.

Al-ummah (الأمّة) is a large group. God Most High said: ﴿And he found upon it a community of people﴾ [28:23]. It is also said of the people of every age that they are an ummah. In the terminology of the theologians (mutakallimīn), the ummah is those who affirm the Messenger ﷺ, not those to whom he was sent, and it is their consensus (ijmā‘) that is taken into account. The intended meaning here is the people of the era.

If you ask: how many communities were there in the interval (fatrah) between ʿĪsā and Muḥammad, peace be upon them both, in which there was no warner? I answer: as long as the traces of warning remained, no community was left without a warner, until those traces were effaced. When the traces of the warning of ʿĪsā were effaced, God sent Muḥammad ﷺ.

If you ask: how did He suffice with mentioning the warner at the end of the verse, rather than the bringer of good news, after mentioning both? I answer: since warning is necessarily accompanied by good news, mention of the one indicates the other, especially as the verse has already included mention of both.

Its colours (ألوانها): their kinds, such as pomegranates, apples, figs, grapes and others that cannot be counted, or their forms, such as red, yellow, green and the like.

Al-judad (الجدد; sing. judda): streaks and stripes. Labid said:

*Or a streak of gold upon its planks*

It is said: the judda of a donkey is the black mark on its back. A gazelle may have two musk-scented streaks that separate the colours of its back and its belly.

﴿وَغَرابِيبُ﴾ (gharabib) is conjoined to ﴿بيض﴾ (white) or to ﴿جدد﴾ (streaks), as if it were said: "And among the mountains are striped ones with streaks, and among them are those of a single colour, gharabib." [[His words "ma huwa ʿala lawn wahid gharabib": perhaps it is gharbib. (ʿ)]] It is related from ʿIkrima, may God be pleased with him, that it means the tall, black mountains.

If you say: gharib is an emphasis of aswad (black). It is said: aswad gharib and aswad ḥalkaws, which is the one that is extremely black and intensely so. From it comes al-ghurab (the crow). Emphasis should follow what it emphasises, as when you say: aṣfar fāqiʿ (bright yellow), abyaḍ yaqiq (pure white), and similar expressions.

I say: its explanation is that the emphasised word is implied before it, and what follows it serves as an explanation of what is implied, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

*By the life of the one around whose Kaaba they circled, and by what was poured out on the idols of blood,*
*and by the protector of birds, which the riders of Mecca watch between Qayl and Sanad,*
*I have never done anything that you dislike; if I have, may I never raise my whip to my hand.*

Al-Nabigha said this, apologising to al-Nuʿman ibn al-Mundhir. The lā before the oath is not superfluous, since it generally serves to negate the claim of an opponent. ʿUmr means life. It is a mubtada' (subject) whose predicate is necessarily omitted. Ṭāfa bihi yaṭīfu ṭayfan means: it came upon him and befell him. Ṭāfa bihi yaṭūfu ṭawafan wa ṭufānan means: he went round it. From it comes ṭayyifa, in the passive. Its deputy subject is the prepositional phrase. Because it is feminine, the verb takes the tā' irregularly, though the eloquent usage omits it in such cases. Al-Ghayl and al-Sanad are two thickets beside Mina. It is also said that they are two watering places on the two sides of the Sacred Precinct, and this is close to what precedes. The meaning is: by the life of the one whom the pilgrims circled around his Kaaba, I swear, and by what was poured out. Al-Muʾmin is in the nominative, conjoined to the subject (ʿUmr). Al-ʿaʾidhat is in the accusative, governed by al-muʾmin. Al-ṭayr is an explicative appositive (ʿatf bayan) to al-ʿaʾidhat. It is also permissible to make it a substitute (badal) for it, and likewise every noun that follows its adjective. Hurriqa is originally uriqa. Al-jasad is the body. Jasada bihi al-dam means the blood clung to him, so he is jāsid and jasad. On the first reading, uriqa means slaughtered. On the second, it keeps its literal sense, but it is a metaphor for slaughter: that which was slaughtered as an offering on the stones set up around the Kaaba. The one who granted safety to the birds that seek refuge in the Sacred Precinct is the one who keeps them under watch while the pilgrims are in Mina, and they do not harm them because they are in the state of iḥram. It is also related as yamsaḥuhā (stroking them), which is more eloquent in expressing security. Mā atayta is the answer to the oath, and in is superfluous. It is also permissible that it is a negation that gives emphasis. Then he invoked a curse upon himself, saying: "If that happens from me, may I never raise my whip to my hand." Yadayya is an explicative appositive. It is a metaphor meaning that he is weakened to the utmost degree. It is also related as sawṭan instead of sawṭī, meaning he is so weakened that he cannot raise it.

This kind of emphasis is used to increase emphasis, since it indicates a single meaning through both explicit and implicit forms together. In the words of God, ﴿وَمِنَ الْجِبالِ جُدَدٌ﴾ ("And among the mountains are streaks"), it is necessary to posit an omitted genitive (muḍāf) so that it means: "and among the mountains are those with streaks, white, red and black", until it returns to your saying: "and among the mountains are those whose colours differ," as He said: ﴿ثَمَراتٍ مُخْتَلِفاً أَلْوانُها﴾ ("fruits of differing colours"). And ﴿وَمِنَ النَّاسِ وَالدَّوَابِّ وَالْأَنْعامِ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوانُهُ﴾ ("And among men and beasts and cattle are those of differing colours") means: "and among them are some whose colours differ."

It is read as ﴿ألوانها﴾ (alwanuha). Al-Zuhri read judad with a ḍamma, the plural of judda, which is jadida, and jadda. It is said: jadida, judad and judaʾid, like safina, sufun and safaʾin. It has been explained in this sense in the verse of Abu Dhuʾayb describing a wild ass:

*Time does not remain upon its ordeals; a dark-backed (or white-backed) wild ass has four she-asses.*

This is from the elegy of Abu Dhuʾayb for his sons. Al-jawn means black, and it is also applied to white, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (aḍdad). Surat al-shay' means its top. Judaʾid means the female asses whose milk has dried up. Al-marʾa al-jaddāʾ is a woman without breasts. He consoles himself for his sons by saying that this is the custom of time, for it does not leave anyone, with all the calamities it contains. The wild ass is described as having four she-asses, with which it grazes in the wilderness and mounts them. It is also said that it lives two hundred years, so one may imagine that time will never harm it. It is permissible to read yabqā with a fatḥa. Jawn with a ḍamma is the subject, and lahu jadaʾid is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: his she-asses must perish one after another, or he himself will perish.

It is also related from him as judad with two fatḥas, which is the clear, manifest road. He placed it in the sense of the clear, distinct paths and lines separated from one another.

It is read as ﴿وَالدَّوَابِّ﴾ with the shortened form (mukhaffafan). A parallel to this shortening is the reading of the one who read ﴿وَلَا الضَّألِّينَ﴾ ("nor of those who go astray"), because each of them is an escape from two consecutive unvoweled consonants: the first of the two is vowelled in one case, and the last of the two is dropped in the other.

His words ﴿كَذلِكَ﴾ mean: like the variety of fruits and mountains. What is meant by "those who know" (al-ʿulamaʾ) are those who know Him through His attributes, His justice and His oneness, and what is permitted of Him and what is not. They magnify Him and esteem Him as He deserves, and they fear Him as He should be feared. The more knowledge one has of Him, the more fear one has of Him, and the less knowledge one has, the safer one is. In a ḥadīth: "The most knowledgeable of you about God is the one who fears Him most." [[I have not found it in this form. In the Ṣaḥīḥ: "I am the most knowledgeable of you about God and the one who fears Him most."]] It is related from Masruq: "It is enough knowledge for a person to fear, and it is enough ignorance for a person to be pleased with his knowledge." A man said to al-Shaʿbi: "Give me a legal opinion, O scholar." He said: "The scholar is the one who fears God." It is also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, when fear of God was manifest in him, so that it was recognised in him.

If you say: does the meaning change if the object is placed first in this sentence or later? I say: it must change. If you put the name of God first and the scholars last, the meaning becomes: "Among His servants, it is only the scholars who fear God, and no others." If you reverse it, the meaning becomes that they fear none but God, as in His words: ﴿وَلا يَخْشَوْنَ أَحَداً إِلَّا اللَّهَ﴾ ("and they fear none but God"). These are two different meanings.

If you ask: what is the connection of this statement to what precedes it? I say: when He said, "Do you not see" (meaning: do you not know) that God sends down water from the sky, and enumerated the signs of God, the indicators of His power, the traces of His craftsmanship, and the varied kinds of creation, through which one is guided to Him and to His attributes, He followed this with: ﴿إِنَّما يَخْشَى اللَّهَ مِنْ عِبادِهِ الْعُلَماءُ﴾ ("Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God"), as if He said: "Only one like you, and one who shares your attributes, fears Him: one who knows Him as He should be known and comprehends the true reality of His knowledge."

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "I hope to be the most God-fearing of you and the most knowledgeable of you about God." [[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from Ibn Jurayj from Zayd ibn Aslam. Mālik in the Muwaṭṭaʾ and al-Shafiʿi from him, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasar, with the same wording, as a mursal report within a ḥadīth beginning: "A man kissed his wife while fasting."]]

If you ask: what is the reasoning behind the reading of those who read ﴿إِنَّما يَخْشَى اللَّهَ مِنْ عِبادِهِ الْعُلَماءُ﴾ with the subject in the accusative (i.e., ﴿اللَّهَ﴾ as the object of ﴿يَخْشَى﴾ and ﴿الْعُلَماءَ﴾ as its subject)? That is ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, and it is related from Abu Hanifa. I say: "fear" in this reading is a metaphor, and the meaning is: "Only those among His servants who are great and honoured (by Him) are held in reverence, just as a dignified man who is feared is held in reverence among people."

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ غَفُورٌ﴾ ("Indeed God is Mighty, Forgiving") is a reason for the obligation of fear, since it indicates His punishment of the disobedient, His subjugation of them, His reward of the obedient and His pardon of them. The one who punishes and the one who rewards deserves to be feared.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 35, verses 32–34:**

If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾? I say: there are two interpretations. The first is that We revealed the Qur'an to you, then We caused it to be inherited after you, that is, We decreed that it be passed down as an inheritance. Or He spoke in the past tense (﴿We caused to inherit﴾) while meaning the present or future (﴿We cause to inherit﴾), as is the custom of God's speech. ﴿Those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾ are His community: the Companions, the Successors, the Successors of the Successors, and those who come after them until the Day of Resurrection. God chose them over all other nations and made them a "middle community" (umma wasat) so that they might be witnesses over mankind. He singled them out with the honour of belonging to the best of God's messengers and of bearing the Book, which is the best of God's books. Then He divided them into: one who wrongs himself (zalim li-nafsihi), who is a sinner and is the one whose affair is deferred to God's command (al-murja'); a moderate one (muqtasid), who mixes righteous deeds with bad ones; and a foremost in good deeds (sabiq), one of the foremost.

The second interpretation is that He mentioned earlier that He sends a messenger to every nation, and that they denied their messengers, even though the messengers had brought them the clear proofs, the scriptures and the illuminating Book. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of God﴾. Thus He praised those who recite His books and act by His laws, out of those among the other nations who denied them. He interposed the statement ﴿And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾, and then said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾, meaning: after those previously mentioned. By "those chosen from His servants" He means the people of the upright (hanifiyya) religion.

If you ask: how did you make ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ a substitute (badal) for ﴿the great bounty﴾, which is the foremost in good deeds, indicated by ﴿that﴾? I say: since the cause of attaining reward is the foremost in good deeds, it is treated as the thing caused, as if it were the reward itself, so the Gardens of Eden are put in its place. In singling out the foremost for mention of their reward after the division, and remaining silent about the others, there is what implies the need for caution: let the moderate one be cautious, and let the one who wrongs himself hold himself in fear, and let both of them turn to God in sincere repentance (tawba nasuh) from the punishment of God. Let them not be deceived by what 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Our foremost is foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven." For the condition of that is the soundness of repentance, so let no one deceive himself with delusions.

[Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This verse began by mentioning those chosen from among God's servants, then divided them into the wrongdoer, the moderate and the foremost, in order to establish that the wrongdoer to himself, from among the monotheists, is included among the chosen, and that he is indeed one of them. What greater and more complete blessing is there than being chosen for monotheism and sound beliefs free from innovations? Why then does the author go to great lengths to equate the chosen monotheist with the audacious unbeliever? His words ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter﴾: the pronoun in "they will enter" refers to the chosen in general, and the Gardens are their reward for their monotheism as a whole. Grammatically: "Gardens" is the subject (mubtada'), and "which they will enter" is the predicate (khabar). His words ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk﴾ to the end of the verse are a predicate after a predicate, and a predicate upon a predicate. And God is the one sought for help.]

[The author's words "so let no one deceive himself" etc. are in the text above.]

Also in the same text: the words of the author regarding the statement ﴿Indeed, the Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter﴾ are as above.

[The author's passage about the reward is as above; the comment on the hadith is as follows: al-Bayhaqi related it in al-Shu'ab from the narration of Maymun ibn Siyah from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, as a marfu' report. This is broken (munqati'). Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh related it by another route, from Maymun ibn Siyah, from Abu 'Uthman al-Hudi, from 'Umar. In it is al-Fadl ibn 'Umayra, who is weak. Sa'id ibn Mansur related it from Faraj ibn Fudala, from Azhar ibn 'Abd Allah al-Harrazi, from one who heard 'Umar, and mentioned it as a mawquf (ending with a Companion) report.]

So the condition of that is the soundness of repentance. [Note: "the soundness of repentance" is the view of the Mu'tazila. As for the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), they permit forgiveness through sheer divine bounty. (Editor's note: ʿ.)]

Because of His words: ﴿It may be that God will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, and His words: ﴿Either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾. The Qur'an has spoken of this in several places, and whoever examines them will come to know the reality of the matter and will not deceive himself with delusions.

It is also read as "sabbaq" (intensive form). The meaning of ﴿by God's permission﴾ is by His facilitation and His granting success.

If you ask: why did He mention the wrongdoer first, then the moderate, then the foremost? I say: to announce the abundance and dominance of the sinners, that the moderate are few in comparison to them, and that the foremost are fewer still than the few.

It is also read as "Jannat 'Adn" in the singular, as if it were a garden specific to the foremost. "Jannat 'Adn" in the accusative is by supposing a verb that the apparent word explains, meaning: they enter the Gardens of Eden, they enter them. "Yadkhuluna" is also read in the passive voice (yudkhalunaha). "Yuhallawna" comes from "huliyat al-mar'a" (the woman was adorned), and is in the state (hal) position. "Wa lu'lu'an" is conjoined to the position of "min asawira" (from bracelets). The word "min" is partitive, meaning: they are adorned with some bracelets of gold, as if this portion precedes the other portions, just as those who were adorned with them preceded others. It is said: that gold is in the purity of pearls. It is also read "wa lu'lu'an" with the first hamza lightened (lu'lu'a → lu'lu'an with softened hamza). The word "al-huzn" (grief) is also read, and what is meant is the grief of the pious: that which concerns them of fear of a bad outcome, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, we were before, among our people, apprehensive. But God has bestowed favour upon us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: the grief of the afflictions and calamities. And from him: the grief of death. From al-Dahhak: the grief of Iblis and his whisperings. It is said: the concern of livelihood. It is said: the grief of the loss of blessings. They have gone far in this, to the extent that some of them said: the rent of the house. Its meaning is that it encompasses every grief of the religion and the world, even this.

From the Messenger of God ﷺ: "There is no loneliness for the people of "There is no god but God" in their graves, nor at their gathering, nor on their journey. As if I see the people of "There is no god but God" coming out of their graves, shaking the dust from their heads, and saying: 'Praise be to God who has removed grief from us.'"

[Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi at the beginning of al-Shu'ab, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related it from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar. In it is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who is weak. It has another route with al-Tabarani and al-Nasa'i in al-Kuna from Ibn 'Umar, and another with al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab. On the subject there is also a report from Ibn 'Abbas, related by Tammam in his Fawa'id and al-Khatib in the biography of Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Ta'ifi; and from Anas with Ibn Mardawayh.]

And the mention of "the Appreciative" (al-Shakur) is evidence that the people are many, and of the good deeds that are established. "Al-Muqama" means "al-Iqama" (residence). It is said: "aqamtu iqama and muqaman and muqama." ﴿From His bounty﴾: from His gift and His bestowal. From the saying: "for so-and-so there is superiority (fudul) over his people, and surpassing qualities (fawadil)." It is not from the "fadl" which means "favour (tafaddul)", because reward is like a due wage, whereas favour is like a voluntary gift.

It is also read "lughub" with a fatha: it is the name of what one becomes weary from, meaning: we do not burden ourselves with a deed that would make us weary; or it is a verbal noun like "al-qabul" and "al-walugh", or an adjective of the verbal noun, as if he said "lughub lughub," like your saying "mawt ma'it" (a dead death). If you ask: what is the difference between "nasab" and "lughub"? I say: "nasab" is fatigue and hardship that befalls one who sets himself to a task and practises it. As for "lughub", it is the languor that follows from the fatigue; so "nasab" is the hardship and burden itself, and "lughub" is its result and what arises from it of weariness and exhaustion.

If you ask: why did they not suffice with *ṣāliḥan* (﴿صَالِحًا﴾, "righteous"), as they sufficed with it in His saying, ﴿فَارْجِعْنَا نَعْمَلْ صَالِحًا﴾ ("return us, that we may do righteousness")? As for the delusion (that they were righteous), it has disappeared, because their condition in unbelief and committing sins was evident. Also, [[His saying "and because they used to suppose" — perhaps it is: "or because they used to suppose." (ʿ)]] they used to suppose that they were on a righteous course, as God, exalted is He, said, ﴿وَهُمْ يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُمْ يُحْسِنُونَ صُنْعًا﴾ ("while they supposed that they were doing good work").
